_comment: The sections of security-notes.md: one for each ASVS requirement that asks for a document and nothing else. `sv notes` writes a section for each that applies, headed by its id, with the question in plain words and what `sv` found that bears on it; the owner writes the answer. A section with an answer makes its requirement *documented*, never *checked*: nothing here reads whether the answer is right, or whether the app does what it says. `title` and `asks` share words with the requirement (crates/sv-check/tests/notes.rs reads them against it), `facts` names what `sv` fills in, and `elsewhere` lists every requirement at level 1 or 2 whose words mention documentation and that has no section here, with why, so a new one cannot be missed silently.

sections.title: What counts as valid input
sections.asks: For each kind of information people type into the app (names, email addresses, dates, amounts, free text), write down the validation rules: what a valid value looks like, how long it may be, and what the app does with one that is not valid.

sections.title: Data items that must make sense combined
sections.asks: Where two or more data items have to agree with each other once combined (a start date before an end date, a city that matches the ZIP code), write down which combinations matter and how the app checks that logical consistency.

sections.title: Business limits
sections.asks: Write down the business logic limits: how many of something one person may create or do, and in how long (per user), and any limits across the whole app (globally), such as a daily total.

sections.title: What files people may upload
sections.asks: For each place people can upload a file: the permitted file types and extensions, the maximum size (including once unpacked, for a zip), and how the app makes a file safe to download again, including what happens when a file looks malicious.

sections.title: How sign-in is protected against guessing
sections.asks: How the app defends against someone trying many passwords (password brute force) or leaked email and password pairs (credential stuffing): rate limiting, delays, or lockout, and the numbers, such as five failed attempts in fifteen minutes. Say how these controls are configured, and how the app stops an attacker locking a real person out on purpose (malicious account lockout).

sections.title: Words not allowed in passwords
sections.asks: A list of context-specific words people may not use in their passwords: the app's name, the organization's name, product names, and other words someone would guess first.

sections.title: Every way to sign in
sections.asks: If there is more than one way to sign in (a password, a Google or Microsoft account, a code by email, an API key), list all these authentication pathways, and say which security controls apply to each, so they are enforced consistently and one is not weaker than the others.

sections.title: How long someone stays signed in
sections.asks: The session inactivity timeout (how long someone can be away before signing in again) and the absolute maximum session lifetime (how long any session lasts at most), and why those times are right for this app. If they are longer than NIST SP 800-63B suggests, say why.

sections.title: Signed in on several devices at once
sections.asks: How many concurrent sessions one account may have at once (a phone and a laptop, say), and what the app does when someone reaches the maximum: sign out the oldest, refuse the new one, or tell the person.

sections.title: Sign-in shared with other systems
sections.asks: If people sign in through a shared system (single sign-on, SSO, a federated identity provider), list every system that creates or manages their sessions, and how session lifetimes and signing out are coordinated between them, including when to ask for re-authentication.

sections.title: Who may do what
sections.asks: The authorization rules: which kinds of users may use which functions (function-level: only administrators may open the admin page), and which records each may see or change (data-specific: a person may only open their own notes).

sections.title: Who may see or change each field
sections.asks: Where some fields of a record are more restricted than the record itself, the field-level access rules: who may read and who may write each field, and whether that depends on the record's state or status (a published order's total can no longer be changed).

sections.title: How keys are looked after
sections.asks: The policy for cryptographic keys: where each key is kept, who can reach it, how often it is replaced, and what happens when one may have leaked, following a key management standard such as NIST SP 800-57 through each key's lifecycle.

sections.title: Every key, algorithm, and certificate
sections.asks: A cryptographic inventory: every key, algorithm, and certificate the app uses, where each key may and may not be used, and what data each may and may not protect. Keep it updated when one is added or replaced.

sections.title: Everything the app talks to
sections.asks: All the communication needs of the app: every external service it connects to (payment providers, email, AI services, other APIs) and why, and any place where someone using the app can give it an address that the app will then connect to itself.

sections.title: How each kind of sensitive data is protected
sections.asks: For each kind of sensitive data the app holds, its protection requirements: whether it is encrypted, how long it is kept (retention), whether and how it may appear in logs, who can see it, and anything the privacy law you follow requires.

sections.title: How quickly outdated libraries are updated
sections.asks: Time frames for remediation: how soon a third-party library with a known vulnerability is updated, by how serious the vulnerability is (for example, critical within a week), and how often libraries are updated in general.

sections.title: Slow or heavy features
sections.asks: Which functionality is time-consuming or resource-demanding (large exports, report generation, AI requests, image processing), and how the app prevents a loss of availability from overusing it: queues, limits per user, timeouts.

sections.title: What the app logs
sections.asks: An inventory of the logging: which events are logged, in what format, where the logs are stored, who can read them (access), what they are used for, and how long they are kept.

elsewhere.why: about output encoding for an HTML document; it asks for no documentation
about escaping JavaScript content; it asks for no documentation
asks for the business limits to be implemented as documented: behavior, which the document in V2.1.3 does not show
about how documents from one site can reach another; it asks for no documentation
about file names keeping a document's structure; it asks for no documentation
asks for the documented list of words to be used when a password is chosen: behavior
asks for the brute-force controls to be implemented as documented: behavior, the running-app half of V6.1.1
asks for multi-factor authentication; documentation is needed only for an exception
asks that no sign-in pathway is undocumented, which is a fact about the app, not the document
asks the app to check an identity provider's claims; documentation is needed only for a fallback
asks for the inactivity timeout to be enforced: behavior, the running-app half of V7.1.1
asks for the absolute session lifetime to be enforced: behavior, the running-app half of V7.1.1
asks for sessions shared with an identity provider to behave as documented: behavior
asks that API documentation is not exposed: a fact about the running app
asks for sensitive data to be protected as documented: behavior, the half of V14.1.2 a document does not show
asks that no component is past its documented update time: checked against the app's packages, not the document
asks for defenses against overuse to be implemented: behavior, the half of V15.1.3 a document does not show
asks that logs go only where the log inventory says: behavior, the half of V16.1.1 a document does not show
asks for the documented security events to be logged: behavior
asks for a DTLS key to be managed as documented: behavior, and only for WebRTC
